results.title: AI infrastructure cost: what's behind a 3-year TCO
results.author: Omar Lari
highlights:
AI infrastructure cost: what's behind a 3-year TCO

October 19, 2026

# AI infrastructure spend: a framework for evaluating cost, risk, and vendor choice

The quoted hourly rate is only part of what AI infrastructure costs. A three-provider study put the three-year gap at 36% against the hyperscaler, split between compute and the team needed to run it, plus four questions to ask before signing.

Omar Lari Senior Director, Product Management

Rohan Mathews Senior Director, Solutions Engineering

Michael YenChi Ho Director, Technical Product Marketing

November 1, 2026

Table of contents

This is some text inside of a div block.

For many teams, AI infrastructure has become a significant line item that deserves the same scrutiny we apply to any other major spend decision. The instinct is to focus on the headline number, the rate a vendor quotes per hour of compute, but that figure is only part of the story. The true cost comes down to three things moving together: the price you're quoted, how much staff time it takes to get the system running and keep it running, and how much useful work you actually get out of it.

An independent study sponsored by Crusoe Cloud "The True Engineering Cost of Open Model Training: A TCO and ROI Analysis of GPU Infrastructure" conducted by Surf Report tested this across three providers, and the results make the case plainly: the provider with the lowest quoted price was not the one that delivered the lowest total cost.

...

The study modeled three-year costs of comparable workloads across Crusoe Cloud, a competing neocloud, and the hyperscaler. The hyperscaler came in with the highest cost at $8.37M, followed by the competing neocloud at $6.14M, and Crusoe Cloud at $5.36M. That's a 56% better ROI for Crusoe Cloud over the hyperscaler, and 15% over the next-best neocloud, worth $3.01M and $780K respectively. But the more interesting number sits underneath those totals.

Roughly $1.27M of Crusoe Cloud's savings compared to the hyperscaler came from staffing rather than the rate card, because running the platform required just under four people, versus more than six on the hyperscaler. That's the practical case for modeling compute cost over years of realistic use rather than a single quote, GPU per hour pricing doesn't reflect the resourcing needed to bring that compute online, and that resourcing is where a meaningful share of the real cost, and the real savings, actually sits.

...

The price per hour of compute answers a singular question only. It tells you what you're charged, not what you get. Two providers can charge the same hourly rate and produce very different amounts of finished work in that hour, depending on how fast and how reliable the system is. A cheaper rate on a slower or less dependable system can end up costing more.

A better metric is cost per unit of completed work, the total spend (compute plus the staff needed to run it) divided by what actually got produced. It's the same logic as any unit-economics analysis: judge cost by output, not by the invoice line. In AI tokenomics terms, this is the shift from a raw hourly rate to cost per token and cost per completed task; measures that capture agent retries and GPU restarts a rate card never shows.

In the study, GPU cost per 1 million training tokens (GPU rate times step time, before staffing and downtime) came in about 13% lower on Crusoe Cloud than on the competing neocloud and about 34% lower than on the hyperscaler. The hourly rate alone would never have shown that gap.

...

A system can look fast on paper and still be expensive in practice if it loses time every time something breaks. The study measured goodput, the share of billed compute time that turns into completed training progress, alongside raw throughput, the tokens-per-second number most teams default to. Throughput counts all the work a system does, including work later lost to a failure and rolled back. Goodput counts the output that actually advances a task toward completion. The test injected three failures, two pod evictions and a node cordon, so recovery time and lost progress are factored in. Goodput also feeds the cost per effective compute-hour, where Crusoe Cloud came in at $9.04 vs. $12.20 on the hyperscaler's matching hardware.

...

and ... providers

...

## Bottom line

The hourly rate is only part of the real cost story. What determines the three-year bill is how many people it takes to run the platform, how much of what you pay for turns into finished work, and how much integration work your own team has to do. On those measures, the independent study found Crusoe Cloud came out ahead, more than a third cheaper than the hyperscaler and modestly cheaper than the next-best neocloud, with a meaningfully higher return over three years, as detailed in the report. It also delivered the lowest cost per training token ($2.89, vs. $3.32 and $4.39) and the highest Goodput under injected failures (99.1%, vs. 94.2% and 95.9%).

Crusoe Cloud integrates orchestration, networking, storage and observability in one control plane, so there is one platform to manage instead of several to reconcile.

...

### How much does AI infrastructure cost?

Total cost depends on staffing and utilization as much as on the quoted hourly rate. "The True Engineering Cost of Open Model Training," an independent Surf Report study of three providers sponsored by Crusoe Cloud, modeled three-year costs of $5.36M on Crusoe Cloud, $6.14M on a competing neocloud, and $8.37M on a hyperscaler for comparable workloads. Roughly $1.27M of Crusoe's advantage over the hyperscaler came from headcount, not rate card.

...

The Surf Report study found compute efficiency and staffing drove the gap, about $1.74M and $1.27M against the hyperscaler.

...

### How much does AI training typically cost?

Cost per GPU-hour understates training cost, because two providers can charge the same rate and finish different amounts of work. A more useful measure is cost per unit of output. On GPU cost per 1 million training tokens, the Surf Report study found Crusoe Cloud about 13% cheaper than a competing neocloud and 34% cheaper than the hyperscaler. Under induced failures, Crusoe Cloud also kept 99% of paid compute productive, versus roughly 94% and 96% for the other two.

results.title: Quantized weights, full precision: The math behind 75% cheaper fine-tuning
results.author: Daniel Shen
highlights:
### What is LoRA fine-tuning?

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tuning customizes a large language model by training small pairs of adapter matrices while the model’s original base weights stay frozen. The adapters usually add 1% or less to the model’s size, so LoRA costs a fraction of full-parameter fine-tuning with minimal quality loss. Crusoe Serverless Fine-Tuning runs LoRA jobs on open models without provisioning GPUs, with billing per training token.

results.title: Crusoe Spark Liquid: 3.5MW modular AI factory | Crusoe
highlights:
October 21, 2026

# Crusoe Introduces Crusoe Spark™ Liquid, Its Next-Generation Modular AI Factory to Power Crusoe Cloud

Prefabricated, closed-loop liquid-cooled Crusoe Spark units deploy in months, adding Crusoe Cloud capacity wherever power and demand exist

November 11, 2026

Table of contents

This is some text inside of a div block.

- Delivers significant compute density engineered for NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, with closed-loop direct liquid cooling 
- Cuts deployment timelines from years to months, adding Crusoe Cloud capacity closer to users for low-latency AI inference
- Crusoe Spark already deployed for Crusoe Cloud customers in production, such as the world’s most popular platform to run open source models, Ollama

DENVER – October 21, 2026 – Crusoe today introduced Crusoe Spark™ Liquid, the sixth generation of its modular AI factory platform. Engineered specifically for the ultra-high-density requirements of next-generation rack-scale systems, including NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, Crusoe Spark Liquid delivers high-efficiency DLC closed-loop cooling to support up to 3.5MW of compute per unit. Units are designed to be deployed in clusters to power AI training and inference at any scale.

Crusoe Spark is a compact modular AI factory data center built in Crusoe's factory and shipped ready to deploy. It is a key growth engine for Crusoe Cloud, scaling capacity rapidly and predictably and bringing it online at lower cost than conventional construction, expanding access to AI compute. Designed for the latest silicon and networking systems, Crusoe Spark shortens data center construction timelines in the field from years to months. 

Built for Crusoe Cloud, Crusoe Spark Liquid units move compute capacity closer to localized demand, providing the low latency essential to real-time inference and agentic AI applications. A single, vertically integrated system that Crusoe builds and operates end to end, Crusoe Spark Liquid unites the company’s modular AI factories and cloud. It delivers the performance frontier AI demands, with NVIDIA Exemplar-level performance for training, along with the data privacy that inference and sovereign AI deployments require. Those efficiencies pass straight through to customers as lower costs and faster deployment. Manufactured in Colorado, Crusoe Spark Liquid will join existing Crusoe Spark production at the company’s Brighton factory in 2027.

...

Crusoe Spark Liquid provides a 5x increase in compute density over previous generations, supporting up to 3.5MW per modular unit. The system utilizes closed- ... non-evaporative ... cooling architecture that delivers full thermal liquid cooling benefits without consuming ... water, ensuring AI companies and enterprise workloads ... scale high-density infrastructure responsibly in water-stressed regions and local communities.

# Crusoe Pledges $50 Million in Compute Credits to White House AI Science Initiative

Crusoe Co-Founder and CEO Chase Lochmiller announces commitment at White House "Science: A New Golden Age" Summit

October 8, 2026

Table of contents

WASHINGTON, D.C. — October 8, 2026 — Crusoe today announced a $50 million commitment in high-performance AI compute credits over three years to support the Genesis Mission Consortium.

Crusoe Co-Founder and CEO Chase Lochmiller announced the pledge at the White House Science: A New Golden Age Summit alongside federal science leaders and industry peers. The contribution will provide capacity for high-performance compute and inference workloads via Crusoe Cloud, the company’s AI cloud platform, as well as technical support to researchers across more than 15 federal agencies, including the DOE, NASA, NIH, and NSF.

results.title: Polar & Crusoe expand Norway AI partnership to 40MW | Crusoe
highlights:
October 21, 2026

# Polar Expands Partnership with Crusoe in Norway with New 40MW AI Infrastructure Development

DRA01 facility now live and powering Crusoe Cloud, as partnership expands into DRA02 to support continued growth of AI infrastructure in Europe

November 11, 2026

...

LONDON, UK – October 21, 2026 – Polar Data Centers (“Polar”), a European developer and operator of AI-ready data center infrastructure, today announced the expansion of its partnership with Crusoe, the AI factory company, building on the successful deployment and operation of Crusoe’s AI infrastructure at Polar’s DRA01 facility in Tørdal, Norway.

DRA01 is now live, providing 12MW of IT capacity, powered by 100% hydroelectric energy. The facility combines modular infrastructure, advanced cooling technology, and resilient electrical systems designed around the requirements of the latest GPU deployments, providing a best-in-class, operational environment to support Crusoe Cloud, Crusoe's AI cloud platform and AI services. The move from initial deployment into stable operations represents an important milestone for the partnership and demonstrates the companies’ ability to deliver and operate infrastructure for the world’s most demanding AI workloads. Polar and Crusoe first announced their partnership around DRA01 in June 2025. 

Building on that success, the companies are now expanding their relationship with DRA02, the next phase of Polar’s Tørdal campus. The new facility, also powered by hydroelectric power, is expected to go live in late 2027, and plans to deliver an additional 40MW of critical, liquid-cooled IT capacity. Crusoe plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 at DRA02 to support the next phase of its AI cloud expansion in Norway. It significantly increases the scale available to support Crusoe Cloud’s continued growth in Europe and beyond.
